slides.title: Precision housings in 2027: keep buying, de-risk the supply, and hold a leased cell as a gated fallback

paragraphs.text: MERIDIAN MOTION  ·  EXECUTIVE COMMITTEE  ·  DECISION PAPER
Precision housings in 2027: keep buying, de-risk the supply, and hold a leased cell as a gated fallback
Answer to: Should Meridian Motion manufacture precision housings in-house in 2027, lease a flexible cell, or continue buying from an external supplier?
For decision at the January 2027 Executive Committee  ·  Prepared November 2026
Based solely on the internal briefing pack; all figures nominal, pre-tax and undiscounted unless stated. Briefing data is synthetic.

slides.title: Keep buying housings in 2027 and spend on supply resilience, not machinery — the owned cell breaks the board's limits and the lease's edge is too thin to bet on

paragraphs.text: Keep buying housings in 2027 and spend on supply resilience, not machinery — the owned cell breaks the board's limits and the lease's edge is too thin to bet on

Continue buying in 2027, convert the single-supplier arrangement into a dual-sourced, capacity-reserved supply with a five-layer outage contingency, pre-qualify a leased cell to be triggered only by pre-agreed gates, and do not build the owned cell.
The owned cell is not a 2027 option

It needs $7.3M against the $5.0M capital limit and would leave ~$3.2M of year-end cash, below the $4.0M floor. The circulated “$27 saving” is $16 per good housing in 2027 once freight, scrap and fixed cost are counted; payback is 3.7 years at 100k units (7.2 at 65k), not “under three”.
Leasing is a cost near-tie that turns negative if any one assumption slips

Over 2027–29 the lease saves $0.3M (1%) versus buying in the planning case, but costs $1.4M more in the conservative demand case and $0.5M more if it runs only seven months of 2027. It needs ≥207k units in 2028–29 just to break even.
Delivery reliability is a supply-design problem that buying can fix faster than any cell

The 0.2-point shortfall (96.8% vs 97% on time) traces to one flood closure. Buffer stock, a tooled alternate shop, 40k reserved units and an emergency supplier act in 0–13 weeks — a cell needs 5–9+ months — for $0.25M of capital and up to $0.72M of working capital.
Pre-agreed gates would switch the answer to the lease; act before the March 2027 quote expiry

Trigger the lease if 2028–29 volume is firmly committed at ≥208k units, the supplier's 2028–29 delivered price exceeds ~$84 (or ~$74 with committed volume), or on-time delivery stays below 97% for two quarters. The plan keeps 2027 year-end cash near $8.2M.
Source: Meridian Motion briefing pack (synthetic data); team analysis (calculations on pp. 6–12 and Appendix A)

paragraphs.text: Four tests the answer must pass
≤ $5.0M new 2027 capital and year-end cash > $4.0M (from $9.2M today, no new debt or equity)
Lowest total cost per good unit over 2027–29, in both planning (300k) and conservative (230k) demand
≥ 97% of units shipped within ten business days, plus an executable outage contingency
Answer holds if demand, scrap, supplier price or start-up timing move against it
The customer mandates delivery reliability and dimensional quality — not insourcing. Housing volumes are not guaranteed: the conservative case cuts 2028 from 100k to 65k units.
Source: Meridian Motion briefing pack (synthetic data) §2–§4. Cost per good unit = cost per start ÷ (1 − scrap rate)

It can be running early enough to protect 2027 deliveries
Five months only if the power/ventilation survey passes → earliest ~June 2027; the supplier quote expires in March (p. 10)
Buying cannot be made reliable enough to meet 97%
96.8% on time, with late orders concentrated in one flood closure; dual sourcing, reserved units and an emergency supplier exist (pp. 10–11)

paragraphs.text: Revised answer: keep buying and make the supply resilient; keep the lease as a gated fallback. The VP's owned cell fails conditions 1 and 2 outright ($7.3M capital; +$1.6M cost in the plan).

slides.title: The circulated “$27 saving per housing” is really $16 in 2027 once freight, scrap and fixed cost are counted, and payback is 3.7 years, not under three

paragraphs.text: The circulated “$27 saving per housing” is really $16 in 2027 once freight, scrap and fixed cost are counted, and payback is 3.7 years, not under three
Owned-cell saving vs buying, $ per good housing, 2027 (80k units, 8% scrap)
$27 × 100k = $2.7M a year; ignores freight, scrap and fixed cost
Undiscounted and pre-tax: adding financing or time value lengthens every payback further. Even with plan volumes, cumulative 2027–29 savings ($5.7M) do not recover the $7.3M.
At steady state (4% scrap, 100k units) the saving is $27.08 − $7.50 fixed = $19.58 per unit. The $75 on the procurement chart is the same quote incl. freight, not a second quote.

slides.title: Building the cell breaches both board limits — $7.3M of capital against a $5.0M cap, and year-end cash of ~$3.2M against a $4.0M floor

paragraphs.text: Building the cell breaches both board limits — $7.3M of capital against a $5.0M cap, and year-end cash of ~$3.2M against a $4.0M floor
Implied year-end 2027 cash vs the $4.0M floor

Even if financed, the owned cell would not help 2027: equipment takes nine months, so first output arrives ~Q4 2027 at the earliest. Cash drops to $1.9M the moment the $7.3M is paid. The 98.5% demo yield that “validates” the cost model excludes start-up runs, rework and three days of tooling downtime; the process engineer plans 8% first-year scrap.
Source: briefing pack §2–§3. Year-end cash = $9.2M − 2027 outflow above today's $6.0M buy spend; rest of business cash-neutral; buy incl. $0.72M buffer

Why the gap is so small: the lease's $49 becomes $51–52 per good unit after scrap, and $1.6M a year of lease and staffing absorbs most of the $23–24 unit margin until volume exceeds ~67k a year.
Why own still loses: its $7.3M upfront is never recovered by 2029 unless a dealer's non-binding $2.1M resale indication comes true.
Source: Meridian Motion briefing pack (synthetic data) §3–§4; team analysis. Totals include upfront cost; full-year 2027 operation assumed for both cells (favours the cells). Detail: Appendix A

slides.title: The reliability gap is 0.2 points and traces to one flood closure — supply levers act in 0–13 weeks, while a cell takes 5–9+ months to arrive

paragraphs.text: The reliability gap is 0.2 points and traces to one flood closure — supply levers act in 0–13 weeks, while a cell takes 5–9+ months to arrive
On-time delivery within ten business days
Weeks until each lever can supply housings
Gap of 0.2 points ≈ 160 housings a year at 80k units
A logistics event, not a capacity gap: the late orders were concentrated in one flood-related road closure.
The customer requires reliability and quality, not ownership; losing the designation would also hit electronics and software sales (unquantified).
Do not rely on the machine-shop correlation: plants with internal shops had fewer delays but also larger, steadier volumes and different products; no before/after evidence isolates the effect.

Implication: the CEO's outage contingency has to come from supply design. Any cell is a 2028 capacity decision, not a 2027 reliability fix — buying capacity early to hedge 2029 is unnecessary when a lease can be stood up in five months.
Source: Meridian Motion briefing pack (synthetic data) §2, §4–§5. Weeks from decision to relief; cell timings exclude ramp-up and assume the site survey passes

slides.title: Each cell's cost per good unit is its per-start cost divided by (1 − scrap), plus fixed and upfront cost — on that basis buying is cheapest or near-cheapest

paragraphs.text: APPENDIX A · COST AND CASH MODEL
Each cell's cost per good unit is its per-start cost divided by (1 − scrap), plus fixed and upfront cost — on that basis buying is cheapest or near-cheapest
Own: $46/start; scrap 8% yr 1, 4% later; $0.75M/yr; $7.3M upfront; ~$2.1M resale after 2029
Year-end 2027 cash, own: $9.2M − ($7.3M upfront + $4.75M 2027 cost − $6.00M buy baseline) = $3.15M; lease: $9.2M − ($2.0M + $5.77M − $6.00M) = $7.43M
Break-even, lease volume: ($2.0M + 2 × $1.6M − $0.23M 2027 saving) ÷ ($75 − $51.04) = 207k units in 2028–29
Break-even, supplier price (plan): ($22.20M − $6.00M 2027 buy) ÷ 220k units = $73.6 per unit in 2028–29; conservative: ($18.63M − $6.00M) ÷ 150k = $84.2
Source: Meridian Motion briefing pack (synthetic data) §3–§4; team analysis. $M nominal; positive “vs buy” = costs more than buying. * $7.3M upfront less $2.1M resale after 2029
